name: Malindi
info: A Swahili city-state ruled by its patrician elders, that received Zheng He's fleet in 1414, welcomed Vasco da Gama in 1498 and rose on the Portuguese alliance to supplant Kilwa and Mombasa.

facts.capital: Malindi; Mombasa from 1593, when the Sheikh of Malindi moved his court there
facts.predecessor: The Swahili settlement of the 5th–10th centuries and the earlier town founded around 850 and destroyed around 1000
facts.successor: Portuguese Mombasa, the main base of the Portuguese in eastern Africa from 1593; the town declined until Sultan Majid of Zanzibar refounded it in 1861

t: Malindi was a Swahili town of coral houses and patrician families whose elders, the wazee, elected a chief, the mwenye mui; the Portuguese mistook these men for kings.

In 1414 the fleet of Zheng He visited the town and Malindi's ruler sent an envoy with a giraffe to China; in 1498 Vasco da Gama was warmly received, after his hostile reception in Mombasa, and raised the pillar that still stands.

Malindi used the Portuguese against its rivals: it supported their conquest of Kilwa and Mombasa in 1505, held their factory from 1502 to 1593, and in 1593 its Sheikh took possession of Mombasa itself.
dyk: Vasco da Gama came to Malindi in 1498 to sign a trade agreement and to hire a guide for the voyage to India; the padrão he erected, the Vasco da Gama Pillar, was in 1823 the only vestige of 'the once splendid city of Melinda' that a British Admiralty chart could find.
ev: After two centuries of sparse habitation following the destruction of the first town around 1000, Malindi recovers and prospers.
Abu al-Fida (1273–1331), the Kurdish geographer, makes the first written reference to the present-day Malindi, south of the mouth of a river rising hundreds of miles inland.
The fleet of the Chinese explorer Zheng He visits the town, and Malindi's ruler sends an envoy with a giraffe as a present to China.
Vasco da Gama meets the Malindi authorities, signs a trade agreement, hires a guide for India and erects a padrão; the town has 5,000 to 10,000 people.
King Dom Manuel I of Portugal offers Malindi vassal status; a Portuguese trading post had been set up in 1499 and a factory follows in 1502.
Malindi supports the Portuguese conquest of its rivals Kilwa and Mombasa, and flourishes as merchants, craftsmen and sailors flock to it.
The Portuguese move their main base to Mombasa, surrendered by the Segeju to the Sheikh of Malindi, who moves his court there and rules until 1630.

sections.foundation:
Malindi grew out of the Swahili civilisation that emerged on the East African coast in the fifth to tenth centuries. Bantu-speaking farmers moved into the area about Malindi Bay, at the mouth of the Galana River, where they smelted iron, built timber and wattle houses thatched with palm leaves, spoke a local dialect of Swahili and traded regionally and at times over long distances. The revival of the Indian Ocean trade at the end of the first millennium brought larger settlements and greater social complexity, and from the eleventh century the Swahili of the coast acted as middlemen for Somali, Egyptian, Nubian, Arab, Persian and Indian traders, built walled towns and coral houses, and saw their elites convert to Islam and often speak Arabic.

The Malindi Kingdom appears to have formed around the ninth century. The first city, founded around 850 somewhat to the north of the modern town, was destroyed around 1000; signs of habitation are sparse for the next two centuries, and recovery and prosperity came in the 1200s. The first written reference is probably that of the Kurdish geographer and historian Abu al-Fida (1273–1331), who placed Malindi south of the mouth of a river rising in a mountain hundreds of miles away, perhaps Mount Kenya, where the Galana rises; the town has thus existed as a Swahili settlement since at least the thirteenth century. Its people converted to Islam largely between the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries.
sections.socioeconomy:
Malindi was a port city whose prosperity rested on the export of ivory and rhinoceros horn and of farm produce, coconuts, oranges, millet and rice. In 1498 it was a prosperous town of between 5,000 and 10,000 people, most of them Muslim. Its society was that of the medieval Swahili towns: the ruling class, the wazee, were the heads of the wealthiest patrician families, who spoke both Swahili and Arabic, built in coral stone and claimed descent from the East. Below them lived the merchants, craftsmen, sailors and labourers of a trading port, and after 1505 the town grew as other Swahili, Arab, Persian and Indian merchants, craftsmen, sailors and labourers flocked to the newly powerful city. The Juma Mosque and other buildings of Swahili architecture survive from the town.

Trade reached far. The fleet of Zheng He called in 1414, and Malindi's ruler sent a personal envoy with a giraffe as a present to China. From 1499 the Portuguese kept a trading post in the town as a rest stop on the way to and from India, and from 1502 to 1593 a factory, and the town was the centre of Portuguese activity in eastern Africa. Before the Portuguese came Malindi was a regional power but lagged well behind the two greatest states of the coast, Mombasa and Kilwa; it was the decline of those two under Portuguese attack that let Malindi flourish. A Portuguese chapel with a graveyard stood before 1542, when Francis Xavier visited the town.
sections.military:
Malindi's strength lay in alliance rather than arms. The town was rivalled only by Mombasa for dominance in its part of East Africa, and the hostility between them shaped its policy: when Vasco da Gama arrived in 1498 after a hostile reception in Mombasa, the Sultan of Malindi received him warmly, signed a trade agreement and supplied a guide for the voyage to India. The wazee eagerly welcomed the trading post the Portuguese established in 1499, seeking to use Portuguese military might to establish themselves over their rivals in Mombasa, and in 1500 King Dom Manuel I offered the town vassal status.

As the chief East African ally of Portugal along the Swahili coast, Malindi supported the Portuguese conquest of the rival powers Kilwa and Mombasa in 1505. The fall of those two cities, the greatest states of the coast, raised Malindi in their place, and the Portuguese factory of 1502 made the town the centre of their activity in eastern Africa for ninety years. The last act of its power was also won by others' arms: in 1592 the Segeju occupied Mombasa and in the end surrendered it to the Sheikh of Malindi, who moved his court there and ruled from 1593 to 1630. He invited his Portuguese allies to build a garrison in Mombasa, and they dominated the city. Malindi's rulers never defeated Mombasa in the field; they outlasted it by choosing the side of the newcomers who did.
sections.governance:
Like the other medieval Swahili towns, Malindi was ruled by its patricians. The ruling class, the wazee, was made up of the heads of the wealthiest families, and, as among other Bantu-speaking peoples, these clan leaders elected a mwenye mui, a chief who spoke on behalf of the patricians. The Portuguese mistakenly titled these men 'kings', misunderstanding the nature of Swahili political organisation, and their accounts speak of the Sultan of Malindi who received Vasco da Gama and of the Sheikh of Malindi who later ruled Mombasa. The wazee spoke both Swahili and Arabic and claimed mythological origins in the East, most often Persia, claims that set them apart from the townspeople and the farmers of the hinterland.

Islam was the religion of government as of the town: the majority had converted between the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, and by 1498 most of the people were Muslim. Diplomacy was the elders' chief instrument. In 1414 the ruler sent his own envoy to China with Zheng He's fleet; in 1498 the authorities signed a trade agreement with Vasco da Gama; from 1500 the town accepted vassal status under the King of Portugal, and a Portuguese factory operated inside it from 1502 to 1593. In 1593 the seat of rule itself moved: the Sheikh of Malindi, given Mombasa by the Segeju, transferred his court there and governed from Mombasa until 1630, with a Portuguese garrison beside him. The old town was left to decline.
sections.impact:
Malindi's choice in 1498 opened the Swahili coast to Portugal. By receiving Vasco da Gama when Mombasa had turned him away, signing a trade agreement and lending him a guide for India, the town gave the Portuguese their first East African ally, a rest stop on the India run from 1499 and a factory from 1502. Its support for the conquest of Kilwa and Mombasa in 1505 helped bring down the two greatest states of the coast and began the Portuguese colonisation of the region, which the historians of the Swahili towns count as the start of their civilisation's decline. For ninety years Malindi was the centre of Portuguese activity in eastern Africa, and its merchants, craftsmen and sailors prospered on the ruin of their rivals.

The town also stood at the far end of China's maritime reach: Zheng He's visit of 1414 and the giraffe sent back to China record a direct exchange between the Swahili coast and the Ming court, and Chinese coins of the fifteenth century lie in the Mambrui dunes. What Malindi built in stone has lasted: the Vasco da Gama Pillar, the Portuguese Chapel built before Francis Xavier's visit of 1542, the House of Columns and the Juma Mosque are heritage sites of the modern town, which remains a largely Muslim community. The transfer of the Sheikh's court to Mombasa in 1593 made that city, with its Portuguese garrison, the pivot of the coast for the centuries that followed.
sections.decline:
Malindi's rise undid it. When the Portuguese moved their main base to Mombasa in 1593, the Sheikh of Malindi, to whom the Segeju had surrendered that city, moved his court there and ruled Mombasa from 1593 to 1630 under the protection of a Portuguese garrison. The factory that had stood in Malindi since 1502 closed the same year. Deprived of its ruler, its Portuguese trade and its place as the centre of their activity in eastern Africa, the old town declined gradually after the Portuguese left, until by the end of the seventeenth century it had almost disappeared.

A British Admiralty chart of 'Melinda' in 1823 declared that there were no vestiges of the once splendid city apart from Vasco da Gama's pillar, and in 1845 the missionary Ludwig Krapf found the town overgrown by vegetation and uninhabited. The buildings of Swahili architecture that survive, among them the Juma Mosque and the Portuguese chapel, date from before this abandonment. Malindi was refounded by Sultan Majid of Zanzibar in 1861 and until the end of the nineteenth century served as a centre of the slave trade; a plan of 1873 shows the area then occupied. In 1890 the town came under British administration, which abolished the slave trade and slavery, and the loss of enslaved labour brought a sharp fall in agricultural production. Officially made a town in 1903, Malindi had about 1,148 people ten years later and grew in the twentieth century into a resort.

summary: Malindi was a Swahili trading town on the Kenyan coast, ruled by its patrician elders, that received Zheng He in 1414 and Vasco da Gama in 1498. As Portugal's chief East African ally it rose on the fall of Kilwa and Mombasa in 1505, held a Portuguese factory for ninety years, and faded when its Sheikh moved his court to Mombasa in 1593.
references: Mark Horton and John Middleton, The Swahili: The Social Landscape of a Mercantile Society (Blackwell, 2000)
Chapurukha M. Kusimba, The Rise and Fall of Swahili States (AltaMira Press, 1999)

notes: The article is about the modern town; the city-state is written from its History section (Swahili origins, the kingdom of c. 850–1000, recovery in the 1200s, Abu al-Fida, Zheng He 1414, da Gama 1498, the wazee and mwenye mui, exports, the Portuguese alliance 1499–1593, the Sheikh in Mombasa 1593–1630, the decline). The military section is thin: the article records no battle fought by Malindi itself.

Register dates 1100–1631: the article gives the kingdom's formation as c. 9th century, the destruction of the first town c. 1000, prosperity from the 1200s, and the Sheikh's rule from Mombasa as 1593–1630. 1100 fits the article's eleventh-century Swahili walled towns only generally; 1631 is one year after the article's 1630. The points keep the register's years.

The article calls the ruler 'Sultan of Malindi' (1498) and 'Sheikh of Malindi' (1593) while also saying the Portuguese wrongly titled the elected mwenye mui 'kings'; the profile uses the article's titles and gives its caveat.
The founder is 'not known': the article names none.

The Mambrui Chinese coins come from the article's tourism section ('15th-century Chinese coins'); the later history (1861 refounding, slave trade, 1890 British rule) is given in the decline section as what followed.
